title: Dogen's Places
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells the story of Dogen's life by place, moving from Mount Hiei and Kennin-ji to China, Koshoji, and Eiheiji. Mary Oliver's poem about setting out to save the only life one can save frames the telling, and Kanho reads from Dogen at each stop, including Valley Sounds, Mountain Colors, One Bright Pearl, Old Mirror with Guotai's answer "An old mirror," and Continuous Practice with Facang's hut. Along the way come the twelve-year-old Dogen running off to the monastery, the lord Hatano Yoshishige giving land for Eiheiji, and Kanho's admission that no record explains why Dogen left Kyoto. Dogen's death poem, written on a follower's wall in 1253, leads into a second Oliver poem about goldfinches in a field of thistles.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good evening.
So good to see you on this beautiful summer evening.
Tonight I will continue with our year of Dogen.
I realized that when I think of Dogen, I just think of him as a monastic sitting zazen and being in his temples.
Then I realized he got around quite a bit.
Even though in a way I thought of him as stationary, he traveled, and his travel was risky and not easy.
It took a long time.
But I considered his travels to be incidental to being a spiritual seeker, searching for a teacher in Japan and China.
I mostly thought of him as residing in monasteries.
So tonight, instead of diving into a specific fascicle, I want to tell you about Dogen coming home.
Perhaps coming home is not the best way of putting it, but it just rang true to me, so I left it like this.
But before you come home, you have to leave, to be gone, to be separated from the home of your heart.
So I will attempt to chronicle the life of that old monk by location.
In this spirit, I would like to offer Mary Oliver's poem, "The Journey."
*The Journey.
One day you finally knew what you had to do, and began, though the voices around you kept shouting their bad advice.
Though the whole house began to tremble and you felt the old tug at your ankles, "Mend my life," each voice cried.
But you didn't stop.
You knew what you had to do.
Though the wind pried with its stiff fingers at the very foundations, though their melancholy was terrible.
It was already late enough in the wild night and the road full of fallen branches and stones.
But little by little, as you left their voices behind, the stars began to burn through the sheets of clouds.
And there was a new voice, which you slowly recognized as your own, that kept you company as you strode deeper and deeper into the world.
Determined to do the only thing you could do, determined to save the only life you could save.*
Dogen Zenji's life was marked by several significant moves, each reflecting a key stage in his spiritual journey and the development of his teachings.
Here is a brief overview of the major changes in location in Dogen's life.
Kyoto, early life and initial training.
Dogen was born in 1200, and at the age of 12 he entered the monastic life.
He began his monastic training at Enryaku-ji, the main temple of the Tendai sect, on Mount Hiei near Kyoto.
Here he studied the doctrines of the Tendai school, but became increasingly dissatisfied with the state of Buddhism in Japan.
His move to the monastery at age 12 was triggered by his family beginning to prepare Dogen for a so-called capping ceremony.
That capping ceremony was going to be the gateway to make him ready for a high-level government position.
Dogen apparently was, even though quite removed, a member of the imperial family, eight times removed.
His great-great-great-great-grandfather was the emperor of Japan.
So Dogen ran off to Mount Hiei, and he asked his uncle, high priest Ryokan, to be allowed to enter the monastery.
Just remember this happened at the ripe age of 12.
When Ryokan found out that Dogen's family had chosen another path, he denied Dogen entry into the monastery.

But Dogen replied, "When my loving mother passed away, she made a request by saying, 'You should go forth from household life and become a student of the way.' Therefore, I do not wish to be involved in the futility of the profane world."

Kōen, the abbot of the Mount Hiei monastery, gave Dogen the Dharma name Dogen, based on a passage in the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Flower Garland Sutra, meaning that faith is the mother of the merit of the original way. [unclear: "Dogen Kodoku"], giving rights to the essential goodness of all beings.
So Dogen did receive the 48 Bodhisattva precepts, typical of the Tendai tradition of the time.
Mount Hiei was the center of Tendai Buddhism in Japan, and a significant place for monastic training.
However, during his time there, Dogen became increasingly dissatisfied with the Buddhist practice he encountered.
He felt that there was an excessive focus on rituals and ceremonies, rather than on the direct experience of enlightenment.
This dissatisfaction eventually led him to seek alternative teachings, which would shape his later spiritual journey and influence his decision to travel to China to find a teacher there.
Now we move to the Kennin-ji Temple in Kyoto.
There, Dogen studied with Myozen.
Dogen felt that he was encountering a more authentic practice there, and it was a Rinzai temple.
Myozen, who was Dogen's teacher, was a disciple of Isai, who was the founder of the Rinzai Zen school in Japan.
He studied there for several years, deepening his understanding of Zen teachings.
I decided that instead of just talking about a fascicle, I would quote a few different passages.
Dogen has two fascicles that I like a lot.
One is Valley Sounds, Mountain Colors, and the other one is One Bright Pearl.
So this is the opening of Valley Sounds, Mountain Colors.
*In the transmission of unsurpassable, complete enlightenment by numberless Buddha ancestors, various practices have arisen.
Study such examples as ancient practitioners crushing their bones and Weike chopping off his arm.
Embody in yourself the dedication of a boy spreading his hair on muddy ground for the Buddha to walk on.
Slipping out of your old skin, not constrained by past views, you manifest immediately what has been dormant for boundless eons.
As this very moment manifests, I don't know.
Who doesn't know?
You have no expectations, and the Buddha eye sees beyond seeing.
This experience is beyond the realm of human thinking.*
And in One Bright Pearl, Dogen brings up this image of this perfect pearl.
This is not quoting Dogen directly, but Stephen Hine in his book *Dogen, Japan's Original Zen Teacher*.
I found this very profound for my own practice.
*To evoke an analogy used by Dogen, it is important that we do not only take into account the pearl that is rolling around in a bowl, which symbolizes an object being examined.
We should also be able to comprehend how the bowl is engaged in turning the gem or the overall framework influencing the topic, including historical investigations and personal reflections.*
So in 1223, Dogen traveled to China together with Miao Zen to seek a deeper understanding of Zen.
They arrived at the port of Ningbo in 1223.
For reasons unknown, Dogen remained on the boat for about three months, then followed with study at various temples.
One of them was a Chan temple on Mount Tian Tong.
He spent time studying with these various masters, but he was not fully satisfied until he met Tian Tong Ru Jing, the abbot of the Jingde temple on Mount Tian Tong.
It seems that Dogen really had the feeling in his heart that he found his true teacher.
He studied intensively there.
It was during that time that Dogen experienced a profound awakening and fully embraced the practice of shikantaza, dropping off body and mind.
He received Dharma transmission from Ru Jing before returning to Japan in 1227.
To this day, scholars have many questions about the journey to China.
Why did Dogen stay on board of the boat for three months?
What about the supernatural experiences Dogen described that he had on the return trip, about meeting Ru Jing and receiving transmission from him?
Probably we will never know, and that's okay too.
So Dogen returned to Japan and first settled down in the Koshoji temple.
He stayed there from 27 until 33.
He began teaching and writing, but he didn't really have the right paperwork to be a teacher.
And he faced resistance from Shingon and Tendai schools in Kyoto.
So in 1233, Dogen established Koshoji, his first temple just south of Kyoto.
He began to gather disciples and teach his understanding of Zen.
This was the first Zen temple in Japan of the Soto lineage.
There he wrote a fascicle related to the theme of moving or migration, titled Kokyo, and it translates into Old Mirror.
This text is one of the fascicles of the Shobu Genzo, Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
I'm sure you all know that by now, but it is a collection of essays on various aspects of Zen practice and philosophy.
In Kokyo, Dogen reflects on the nature of movement and change, not just in the physical sense, but also in the spiritual and existential sense.
He uses the metaphor of an old mirror to explore the themes of impermanence, the continuity of practice, and the idea of returning to one's original nature.
The old mirror symbolizes the true self, which remains constant and clear despite the changes and movements that occur in life.

While this fascicle is not directly about the physical act of moving from one location to another, it deals with the underlying philosophical and spiritual implications of movement and change and returning to one's own essence.
Dogen's reflections in this text can be seen as a metaphor for his own life, including his decision to move from Kyoto to the more remote Echizen province to establish a Eiheiji temple.

If you're thinking of a fascicle that deals more directly with the idea of migration or moving in a literal sense, Dogen's writings often touch on the broader theme of leaving home, shukke, in the context of monastic life, which involves leaving behind earthly life and attachments to pursue the path of Zen.
Let me read you a little bit from Kokyo.
*Guotai Zen Master Huang Tao of the Guotai Monastery, Mount Xinhua, Wu region, was asked by a monk, "What is an old mirror that is not yet polished?"
Guotai said, "An old mirror."
The monk asked, "What is an old mirror that is already polished?"
Guotai said, "An old mirror."
Know that the old mirror spoken of now is an old mirror throughout the time when it is polished, before it is polished, and after it is polished.
Thus, when you polish it, you polish the entire old mirror.
It is not that you apply mercury or something else to an old mirror and polish it.
Also, it is not the self polishing or polishing the self.
It is polishing an old mirror.
You polish a mirror and make it a mirror.
You polish a tile and make it a mirror.
You polish a tile and make it a tile.
You polish a mirror and make it a tile.
Also, you polish but do not accomplish, or you accomplish but do not polish.
These are all works in the house of Buddha ancestors.*

So in 1243, Dogen apparently faced increasing opposition and dissatisfaction with the environment in Kyoto, and Dogen accepted an invitation from Hatano Yoshishige, a local lord, to move to Echizen province, modern-day Fukui Prefecture.
Remember that name, Hatano Yoshishige.
He made basically Ehechi possible.
There were probably several factors, both personal and religious, which drove Dogen to seek a more conducive environment for his practice and teachings.
There were religious and political conflicts.
Kyoto was a center of power struggles and religious politics.
Established sects such as Tendai and Shingon were dominant, and they often resisted new teachings or movements that challenged their authority.
Dogen's teachings, which emphasized the return to the original unadorned practice, were seen as a threat by these established sects.
This made it difficult for Dogen to gain a strong following and to establish his teachings.
At the same time, I misunderstood this for the longest time.
I thought there was really a movement to drive Dogen out of Kyoto.
However, there is no documented reason why he did leave in the end.
Like I said, I thought it was a rivalry between sects, but it doesn't show up anywhere in the Shobogenzo or other writings that there was a specific cause.
It's another thing that will be a mystery forever.
But different thoughts come up for people.
One was a desire for a better practice environment.
So probably Dogen saw the place where he and his followers could practice without the distractions and corruptions of urban life and political entanglements.
For a while he was striving to become one of the temples that are acknowledged by the emperor, and he named his temple like for the safety of the empire.
But he did get rid of that part after that didn't seem to work out.
So a natural environment would probably be more conducive to the rigorous Zen practice he advocated.
So they established Ehechi in Echizen province in 1244.
Ehechi was far from the political and religious pressures of Kyoto, allowing a focus on developing the Soto Zen school without interference.
The remote mountainous location of Ehechi embodied the simplicity and purity that Dogen perhaps sought for his new practice environment.
Dogen may also have been disillusioned with the spiritual atmosphere of Kyoto, which he saw as overly concerned with ritual power and prestige rather than direct experience.
By leaving the capital he distanced himself from these influences, and he began to teach a more authentic practice-oriented Zen.
So Dogen started to cultivate this new community, and he also described quite a bit of monastic life in Shobogenzo, from how to scrape your tongue, clip your fingernails, wipe your butt, everything.
It's in Shobogenzo.
The escape from the political conflict allowed him to just practice.
One of the themes of practice is that it does not end.
There are two beautiful fascicles in Shobogenzo called Continuous Practice, and I would like to tell you a little bit about that.
*On the great road of Buddha ancestors, there is always unsurpassable practice, continuous and sustained.
It forms the circle of the way and is never cut off.
Between aspiration, practice, enlightenment and nirvana, there is not a moment's gap.
Continuous practice is the circle of the way.
This being so, continuous practice is undivided, not forced by you or others.
The power of this continuous practice confirms you as well as others.
It means your practice affects the entire earth and the entire sky in the ten directions.
Although not noticed by others or by yourself, it is so.*
So as I said before, Dogen was invited by Hatano Yoshishige, a local lord in Echizen province, to move to the area.
Hatano offered Dogen land and resources to establish a temple, and he continued to sponsor the temple throughout its existence.
This support was crucial for Dogen as it allowed him to create a monastic community that was independent of institutions in Kyoto.
Dogen's move to Ehechi was also driven by his long-term vision of establishing a lasting legacy for his teachings.
He wanted to create a place where his understanding of Zen could be preserved and transmitted to future generations.
And look, here we are.
Ehechi was to be a temple where monks could dedicate themselves entirely to the practice of Zen, embodying the principles that Dogen had learned from his Chinese teacher, Lu Jing.
Another little piece of Continuous Practice.
*After many years, a monk from the assembly of Yanguan went to the mountain looking for wood to make a staff.
He lost his way and after a while found himself in front of Facang's hut.*
Facang was a pretty famous teacher.
*Seeing Facang, he asked, "How long have you been on this mountain?"
Facang said, "I have seen nothing but the green and yellow of the surrounding mountains."
The monk said, "How do I get off this mountain?"
Facang said, "Follow the stream."
Mystified by Facang, the monk went back and told Yanguan about him.
Yanguan said, "When I was in Jiangji, I saw a monk like that, but I haven't heard of him since.
This might be him."
Yanguan sent the monk to Facang and invited him to come to the monastery.
Facang would not leave the mountain, but responded with a poem.
"A decayed tree remains in the cold forest.
Meeting springs, there is no change of mind.
Woodcutters see me, but I ignore them.
How come the woodmaster seeks me out?"*
So Dogen believed that the natural environment played a crucial role in spiritual practice.
The serene and secluded settings of Eiheiji, surrounded by mountains and forests, were seen as an ideal place to engage deeply in practice.
This connection to nature was an important aspect of Dogen's teachings.
Dogen Zenji had several important sponsors throughout his life, but the most significant was that Hatano Yoshishige I mentioned.
He donated the land on which Dogen founded Eiheiji in 1244.
This donation was critical in allowing Dogen to move away from Kyoto, so we should have great gratitude to Hatano Yoshishige.
He also protected the monastery and helped sustain the temple and the followers who moved there.
His relationship with Dogen was more than just patron and abbot.
It was a genuine partnership based on mutual respect.
Hatano admired Dogen's teachings and was committed to helping him, so it was mostly through his sponsorship that this lasting legacy was created.
Eiheiji remains one of the two head temples of Soto Zen in Japan, continuing the tradition that Dogen established nearly 800 years ago.
Now I'm moving on to the later years at Eiheiji.
Dogen continued to engage with Shobogenzo.
He started to rewrite several fascicles with a goal to finish up with a 100-fascicle Shobogenzo edition.
There's also a Shobogenzo Zuimonki, record of things heard, and it was his successor Ejo who wrote Shobogenzo Zuimonki based on Dogen's informal Dharma talks.
Dogen continued to teach and write until his health declined.
In 1253 his health had declined, and he traveled back to Kyoto to seek medical treatment.
In Kyoto he stayed at the house of a lay follower, and he passed away shortly after, at the age of 53.
He wrote his death poem on the wall in his follower's house, and this is it.
*For 53 years, following the way of heaven, now leaping beyond, shattering every barrier, amazing, I cast off all attachments.*
That's pretty much the end of my talk, but I thought I'd give you a little poem by Mary Oliver to close the invitation.
*Oh, do you have the time to linger for just a little while out of your busy and very important day?
For the goldfinches that have gathered in the field of thistles, for a musical battle to see who can sing the highest note or the lowest or the most expressive of mirth or the most tender.
Their strong, blunt beaks drink the air as they strive melodiously, not for your sake and not for mine, and not for the sake of winning but for the sheer delight and gratitude.
"Believe us," they say, "it is a serious thing.
Just to be alive on this fresh morning in the broken world."
I beg of you, do not walk by without pausing to attend to this rather ridiculous performance.
It could mean something.
It could mean everything.
It could be what Rilke meant when he wrote, "You must change your life."*
Thank you very much for listening to this talk.
